content: The trial was terminated in 2011 after an interim analysis concluded that it was unlikely to detect a statistically significant difference in efficacy between the two study groups. Adherence to the study drug was low, with plasma samples showing detectable levels of the drug in less than 50% of women assigned to the TDF/FTC group. Adverse events such as nausea and vomiting (primarily in the first month) and transient, modest elevations in liver function test values were more common in the TDF/FTC group compared to the placebo group. No changes in renal function were observed in either group. Among the 68 women who acquired HIV during the trial, TDF or FTC-resistant virus was detected in five women: one in the placebo group and four in the TDF/FTC group. Multivariate analyses showed no association between pregnancy rates and study group assignment. A Phase 2 trial of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir (TDF) was conducted among heterosexual women in Ghana, Cameroon, and Nigeria to evaluate the safety of TDF use and its efficacy in reducing HIV infection rates. The study sites in Cameroon and Nigeria were prematurely closed due to operational challenges, resulting in insufficient follow-up data for planned efficacy analysis. Safety data from Ghana and Cameroon revealed no statistically significant differences in grade 3 or 4 hepatic or renal events or in reports of clinical adverse events. Blood specimens from one of the two participants who seroconverted while taking TDF showed no evidence of drug-resistance mutations upon genotypic analysis. The VOICE (Vaginal and Oral Interventions to Control the Epidemic) trial was a Phase 2B randomized, double-blind study comparing oral (TDF or TDF/FTC) and topical vaginal (tenofovir) antiretroviral regimens against corresponding placebos among 5,029 heterosexual women in eastern and southern Africa. In 2011, the oral TDF and topical tenofovir groups were discontinued after interim analyses indicated futility. The oral TDF/FTC group continued to the planned trial conclusion. After excluding women with acute HIV infection at enrollment and those with no follow-up visits, 52 incident HIV infections occurred in the oral TDF group, 61 in the TDF/FTC group, and 60 in the oral placebo group. Adherence to medication, as assessed by interviews, self-reports, and pill counts, was high (84%-91%) across all groups. However, plasma samples from a random cohort showed detectable tenofovir in only 30% of women in the TDF group and 29% in the TDF/FTC group, with no drug detected in 58% of women in the TDF group and 50% in the TDF/FTC group at any quarterly visit. The percentage of samples with detectable drug levels was less than 40% in all study drug groups and declined over time. Multivariate analysis adjusting for baseline confounders found no association between detectable drug levels and reduced HIV acquisition risk. Confirmed creatinine elevations were more frequent in the oral TDF/FTC group than in the placebo group, but no significant differences were observed for other safety outcomes. Among women with acute HIV infection at baseline, two in the TDF/FTC group had virus with the M184I/V mutation associated with FTC resistance. One woman in the TDF/FTC group who acquired HIV after enrollment also had virus with the M184I/V mutation. No participants had virus with mutations associated with tenofovir resistance. In summary, low adherence and operational challenges limited reliable conclusions regarding efficacy in three trials (VOICE, FEM-PrEP, and the West African trial). However, two trials (Partners PrEP and TDF2) with high medication adherence provided substantial evidence of efficacy among heterosexual men and women. All five trials demonstrated the safety of PrEP in these populations. Daily oral PrEP with TDF/FTC is recommended as an HIV prevention option for heterosexual men and women at substantial risk of HIV acquisition, as these trials provide evidence of its safety and, in two cases, efficacy, particularly when adherence is high.
